'''Douglas Geoffrey Northcott''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (31 December 1916 – 8 April 2005)<ref name="Sharp">{{Cite journal | last1 = Rees | first1 = D. | last2 = Sharp | first2 = R. Y. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2007.0010 | title = Douglas Geoffrey Northcott. 31 December 1916 -- 8 April 2005: Elected FRS 1961 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 53 | pages = 247 | year = 2007 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/338/338_07.html|title=Douglas Northcott at the London Mathematical Society (LMS)|access-date=2011-07-20|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012060415/http://www.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/338/338_07.html|archive-date=2007-10-12}}</ref> was a British [[mathematician]] who worked on [[ideal theory]].

==Early life and career==
Northcott was born Douglas Geoffrey Robertson in Kensington on 31 December 1916 to Clara Freda (née Behl) (1894–1958) and her first husband Geoffrey Douglas Spence Robertson (1894–1978). His mother remarried in 1919 to Arthur Hugh Kynaston Northcott (1887–1952). In 1935, he legally adopted his step-father's surname.<ref name="Sharp" />

He was educated in London, then at [[Christ's Hospital]] and [[St John's College, Cambridge]], where he started research under the supervision of [[G.H. Hardy]].

His work was interrupted by active service during [[World War II]]. Captured at Singapore, he survived his time as a prisoner of war in Japan, and returned to Cambridge at the end of the war.

Back at Cambridge, he published his dissertation "Abstract Tauberian theorems with applications to [[power series]] and Hilbert series ".<ref name=mactutor>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Northcott}}</ref><ref>{{mathGenealogy|160562}}</ref>  He then turned to algebra under the influence of [[Emil Artin]], whom he had met while visiting [[Princeton University]]. He became a Research Fellow of St John's College in 1948.

In 1949, he proved<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Northcott |first=Douglas |date=1949 |title=An inequality in the theory of arithmetic on algebraic varieties |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0305004100025202/type/journal_article |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |language=en |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=502–509 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100025202 |bibcode=1949PCPS...45..502N |issn=0305-0041|url-access=subscription }}</ref> an important result in the [[Height function|theory of heights]], namely that there are only finitely many algebraic numbers of bounded degree and bounded height. In analogy to this result, a set of algebraic numbers is said to satisfy the Northcott property if there are only finitely many elements of bounded height. <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Checcoli |first1=S. |last2=Fehm |first2=A. |date=2021-03-26 |title=On the Northcott property and local degrees |url=https://www.ams.org/proc/2021-149-06/S0002-9939-2021-15411-7/ |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |language=en |volume=149 |issue=6 |pages=2403–2414 |doi=10.1090/proc/15411 |issn=0002-9939|arxiv=2005.10609 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Widmer |first=Martin |date=2011 |title=On certain infinite extensions of the rationals with Northcott property |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00605-009-0162-7 |journal=Monatshefte für Mathematik |language=en |volume=162 |issue=3 |pages=341–353 |doi=10.1007/s00605-009-0162-7 |issn=0026-9255|arxiv=1205.2491 }}</ref>

In 1952, he moved to the [[Sheffield Town Trust|Town Trust Chair]] of Pure Mathematics at [[Sheffield University]]. He remained at Sheffield until his retirement in 1982, also serving as Head of Department and Dean of Pure Science.

In 1954, Douglas Northcott and [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]] introduced in a joint paper<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1017/S0305004100029194 | last1=Northcott | first1=D. G. | last2=Rees | first2=D. | authorlink2=David Rees (mathematician) | title=Reductions of Ideals in Local Rings | journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] | volume=50 | number=2 | pages=145&ndash;158 | year=1954 | bibcode=1954PCPS...50..145N | s2cid=123098860 }}</ref> the Northcott-Rees theory of reductions and integral closures, which has subsequently been influential in [[commutative algebra]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-douglas-northcott-220370.html | location=London | work=The Independent | title=Professor Douglas Northcott – Obituaries, News – The Independent}}</ref>

==Awards==
Northcott was awarded the [[London Mathematical Society]] Junior [[Berwick Prizes|Berwick Prize]] in 1953 and served as LMS Vice-President during 1968-69. He was elected [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1961.

==Family life==
In 1949, at Cambridge, Northcott married Rose Hilda Austin (1917-1992), with two daughters, Anne Patricia (born 1950) and Pamela Rose (1952-1992).

== Publications ==
* Northcott, D. G. ''Multilinear algebra.'' [[Cambridge University Press]], Cambridge, 1984. {{ISBN|0-521-26269-0}} 
* Northcott, D. G. ''A first course of homological algebra.'' Reprint of 1973 edition. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge-New York, 1980. {{ISBN|0-521-29976-4}}
* Northcott, D. G. ''Affine sets and affine groups.'' London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series, 39. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge-New York, 1980. {{ISBN|0-521-22909-X}} 
* Northcott, D. G. ''Finite free resolutions.'' Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics, No. 71. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge-New York-Melbourne, 1976. 
* Northcott, D. G. ''Lessons on rings, modules and multiplicities.'' Cambridge University Press, London 1968
* Northcott, D. G. ''An introduction to homological algebra.'' Cambridge University Press, New York 1960 
* Northcott, D. G. ''Ideal theory.'' Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics and Mathematical Physics, No. 42. Cambridge, at the University Press, 1953.
